gain.title: Every brain of round 3 responds
gain.caption: Each dot is a living world of round 3, placed by its brains' shape: the median, over 300 of its agents, of how much a small change of every input reaches the outputs — every input moved by a normal amount of standard deviation 0.1, and the root-mean-square change of the outputs over that of the inputs, the brain's gain. Blue: the agents' own brains at the end of the world; grey: fresh founders' brains of the same shape (weights normal with standard deviation 1/√(fan-in), biases 0) shown exactly the same inputs; the bar is the median. The dashed lines are B1's five sigmoid layers ([What the brains are like](what-the-brains-are-like.md)).

Left: every neighbour's tokens, as the agent sees them, doubled; middle: the random numbers of every column drawn again (only in worlds whose brains read random numbers); right: every message read set to 0 (only in worlds with messages). Grey: fresh founders' brains; cyan: founders' brains taken to mutation's balance, where its changes alone would bring them, with nothing selected (see the text); blue: the agents' own brains; the bar is the median. The dashed line is B1's evolved brains.

**Runs.** Round 3 of the random screen: Experiment 40's 84 worlds, each a draw of its own, and the 16 of Experiments 41 and 42, eight draws played twice with the stakes placed a token at a time (30,000 tokens, 3,000 iterations; [A screen of random worlds](a-screen-of-random-worlds.md))

evolution.title: What evolution did to the gain
evolution.caption: Left: the brains of every world kept along the way (one every 250 iterations, the founders first, the agents' own at the end) shown the same inputs, those of the world's end, and their gain over the founders' gain; the line is the median of the 82 living worlds, the band holds the middle half of them. The upper dashed line is the median gain, over the founders', of founders' brains taken to mutation's balance: where its changes alone would bring them after very many, with nothing selected. Middle: one dot per world, the gain of its evolved brains against that of brains at its mutation's balance; on the dashed line the two are equal. Right: each world's evolved weights, the median over layers of their size as a multiple of a founder's, against the size mutation alone would bring them to.
evolution.recipe:
**Runs.** Round 3 of the random screen: Experiment 40's 84 worlds, each a draw of its own, and the 16 of Experiments 41 and 42, eight draws played twice with the stakes placed a token at a time (30,000 tokens, 3,000 iterations; [A screen of random worlds](a-screen-of-random-worlds.md))

**Data.** From each living world's checkpoint, `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/checkpoint.npz` (the world after its last iteration), and its archive, `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/archive/world_<iteration>.npz` (the whole world every 250 iterations, from the founders on), read by `book_chapters.brainsize.kept_world` with the brains of the agents probed only.

1. For 300 agents drawn at random among those holding a token or more (seed 53), their inputs exactly as the engine builds them for a look at their candidates (`World._precompute_features`, `World._inputs`).
2. For every kept world of the run, 300 brains of agents holding a token, drawn at random (seed 5304 + the iteration), each shown one agent's inputs; their gain as for the figure above.
3. Mutation's balance (`balance`): a change jitters a share s of the numbers by a normal amount of standard deviation σ/√k and, with chance s, redraws a share s of a matrix at the founders' 1/√k; the variance of a weight settles at (1 + (1 − s²)σ²/s)/k, and of a bias at σ²(1 + (1 − s²)/s)/k. A founder's weights scaled to it, and biases drawn at it (`drifted`).
4. The weights' size: the root mean square of a layer's weights times √(fan-in), the median over the layers and the agents.

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py brainsize`.

change.title: How far one change moves a brain
change.caption: One dot per living world, by the depth of its brains: how much one change of a brain ([How a brain changes](rules-in-detail.md#how-a-brain-changes), made for sure, with the world's own settings) moves the outputs that make decisions, over how much the brain of a stranger differs from it, on the same inputs — the root-mean-square differences, the median over the agents probed. Grey: fresh founders' brains, each against another founder's; blue: the agents' own brains at the end, each against another agent's of the same world; the bar is the median. The dots high above the rest are the worlds whose changes touch three numbers in ten (a mutation sparsity of 0.3).
change.recipe:
**Runs.** Round 3 of the random screen: Experiment 40's 84 worlds, each a draw of its own, and the 16 of Experiments 41 and 42, eight draws played twice with the stakes placed a token at a time (30,000 tokens, 3,000 iterations; [A screen of random worlds](a-screen-of-random-worlds.md))

**Data.** From each living world's checkpoint, `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/checkpoint.npz` (the world after its last iteration), and its archive, `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/archive/world_<iteration>.npz` (the whole world every 250 iterations, from the founders on), read by `book_chapters.brainsize.kept_world` with the brains of the agents probed only.

1. For 300 agents drawn at random among those holding a token or more (seed 53), their inputs exactly as the engine builds them for a look at their candidates (`World._precompute_features`, `World._inputs`).
2. Each brain changed once with the world's own mutation settings (seed 5305; `mutated`), and both shown the agent's inputs; the stranger is the agent probed half the sample away in the order of their ids, so that it was born far from it in time.

worlds.title: What the shape did to the worlds
worlds.caption: Experiment 40's worlds by the depth of their brains (orange: 3, 4 or 5 hidden layers) and by their width (green: 16, 32 or 50 units a layer): the share that died, of all 84; and for the 70 living worlds, one dot each with a bar at the median, their health (the six criteria multiplied, as their geometric average), how much children act like their parents, how many generations they lived in 3,000 iterations, their effective population, and how far their line of descent kept moving into new behaviour ([Candidates for open-ended evolution](candidates-for-open-ended-evolution.md#how-each-pillar-is-read)). The table below gives, for each, the chance by shuffling of a trend with depth or with width at least as strong, with the settings already known to matter for that outcome taken into account.
worlds.recipe:
**Runs.** Round 3 of the random screen: Experiment 40's 84 worlds, each a draw of its own, and the 16 of Experiments 41 and 42, eight draws played twice with the stakes placed a token at a time (30,000 tokens, 3,000 iterations; [A screen of random worlds](a-screen-of-random-worlds.md))

**Data.** From each world's drawn settings (its plan, `book/experiments/E40.json`, drawn by `gol_screen.py`) and what the screen measured of it: whether it died, and for the living its health (`research/screen/health.json`) and how it evolved (`research/screen/effects.json`, from each world's dossier).

1. For each outcome, the settings whose own shuffling test on it had a chance below 0.05 ([How the drawn settings shape a world](how-the-drawn-settings-shape-a-world.md)), and the other of depth and width.
2. Rank the outcome over the worlds; take away a least-squares fit of the ranks on those settings' values (one column of 0 and 1 per value); correlate what is left with the rank of depth (or width).
3. The chance: the share of 20,000 shuffles of depth (or width) among the worlds (seed 53) giving a correlation at least as far from 0 (`shape_test`).

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py brainsize`.
